newsitem.title: USA: It's official -- Clinton, Gore won!.
newsitem.headline: It's official -- Clinton, Gore won!.

text.p: Two months and four days after November's U.S. election, the outcome is now official: President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore won.
Their victory margin: 379 electoral votes to 159 for Republicans Bob Dole and Jack Kemp and none for anyone else.

This was duly certified and announced for the record, and for really finicky historians, on Thursday at a 25-minute joint session of Congress. There, as required by the U.S. Constitution, the votes cast by members of the Electoral College in December were read and counted.

Under the indirect U.S. election system that confuses people every four years, the electors from each of the 50 states were chosen on Nov. 5 when Americans voted for slates pledged to either Democrats Clinton and Gore, Republicans Bob Dole and Jack Kemp or any of the many other candidates.
There are a total of 538 electors, with each state getting the same number as represented in its congressional delegation plus three for Washington, D.C.
Only a handful of House and Senate members were present as the certificates of electoral votes from all over were opened and read.
The public galleries were half empty but attendence may have been hurt by snow that hit Washington on Thursday morning.
Gore, in his role as presiding officer of the Senate and chairman of the meeting, got to read the results.
They were the same as widely calculated and reported on election night, 379-159.
Reform Party leader Ross Perot and other presidential candidates did not win any electoral votes.

"This announcement shall be deemed a sufficent declaration of the persons elected president and vice president of the United States, each for the term beginning on the 20th day of the January, 1997, and shall be entered together with a list of the votes on the journals of the Senate and House of Representatives," Gore intoned, reading the traditional script.
Although famous for a wooden speaking style, not even he actually talks like that.
Clinton will be sworn-in for a second term as president on inauguration day, January 20.

The Electoral College was established by the Constitution in 1789. Proposals are made after each presidential election to abolish it and use the popular vote, but that would require a constitutional amendment and none has ever been approved.
